• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner uses a cylinder and a cone of the same radius and height, and a substance such as sand or water, to determine the volume of a cone as a third of the volume of a cylinder. In this unit learners also the learner analyses composite solid shapes found in real-life Kenyan contexts — such as grain silos in Eldoret or water tanks in rural Rift Valley — and decomposes them to determine total surface area and volume.
• Creativity and Imagination: the learner uses a cylinder and a cone of the same radius and height, and a substance such as sand or water, to determine the volume of a cone as a third the volume of a cylinder. In this unit learners also improvises and constructs nets and models of prisms, pyramids, cones and spheres using locally available materials (cardboard, manila paper) to verify surface area formulae.
• Also practised in this unit (not named in the KICD design for this sub-strand):
• Communication and Collaboration: the learner discusses and shares findings with peers when measuring and calculating the surface area and volume of locally available solid models such as tins, packets and containers used for ugali flour or cooking oil.
• Digital Literacy: the learner uses digital devices and software (where available) to explore 3D solid models, nets and volume visualisations.
• Self-Efficacy: the learner builds confidence in applying surface area and volume formulae independently to solve real-world packaging, construction and storage problems relevant to Kenyan industries.

records.old: A sphere is best of all, so artisans choose
records.new: A sphere is best of all: made into a sphere, the same 30,800 cm2 of sheet would have r = 49.5 cm (4 x 22/7 x r2 = 30,800 gives r2 = 2,450) and hold about 508 litres (4/3 x 22/7 x r3), more than the drum's 404.25 litres. Even so, artisans choose
records.group_headline: 'A sphere is best of all' and the Lesson 8 sphere prediction were never tested; now checked with numbers (30,800 cm2 as a sphere holds about 508 litres)
records.why: The unit repeatedly says a sphere is best of all and Lesson 8 asks learners to predict it, but nobody ever calculates it, and Lesson 6 calls it 'established'. Checked twice: 4 x 22/7 x r2 = 30,800 gives r2 = 30,800 x 7 / 88 = 2,450, r = 49.497 cm; V = 4/3 x 22/7 x 49.497^3 = 508,174 cm3 (508 litres); using exact pi the answer is 508,276 cm3, so 'about 508 litres' holds. 508 > 404.25 litres, so the claim is true for these numbers.
records.reference: Isoperimetric inequality for solids: among all solids with a given surface area the sphere has the greatest volume (e.g. Courant and Robbins, What Is Mathematics?, chapter on maxima and minima)

records.old: Ask: 'A sphere is best of all, so why does Wanjiru not make spherical tanks for grain?'
records.new: First test the Predict-phase sphere prediction with the class: 'If Wanjiru bends 30,800 cm2 of sheet into a sphere, what is r, and what does it hold?' (4 x 22/7 x r2 = 30,800, so r2 = 2,450 and r is about 49.5 cm; V = 4/3 x 22/7 x r3 is about 508,000 cm3, about 508 litres, more than the drum's 404.25 litres.) Then ask: 'A sphere is best of all, so why does Wanjiru not make spherical tanks for grain?'
records.why: Knock-on edit of the sphere test: gives teachers the worked check and the expected numbers.
records.reference: Isoperimetric inequality for solids (sphere has the greatest volume for a given surface area); see group root.

records.why: Lesson 6 called the sphere result 'established' although nothing in the unit had shown it. It is now told as a fact to be tested in Lesson 8.

value.criterion: Calculating surface area and volume correctly
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Uses the correct method for each solid (prism, cylinder, pyramid, cone, sphere, composite), uses slant height and vertical height correctly, gets all values right (30,800 cm2; 404,250 cm3; 322,500 cm3) with correct units and working.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses mostly correct methods and gets most values right, with one or two small slips in arithmetic, units or choice of height.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Confuses formulae, mixes slant and vertical height, or omits working and units, so the values are mostly incorrect.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: States clearly that surface area is the material covering a solid and volume is the space inside, and correctly classifies each task as a surface area or volume question with reasons.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Distinguishes the two ideas correctly but gives limited reasons or misclassifies one task.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Treats surface area and volume as the same thing or cannot say which one a task needs.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Explains why the drum holds 81.75 litres more than the box using the shared 30,800 cm2, both volumes and the cross-section areas (3,850 cm2 against 2,500 cm2), noting that the drum's larger base outweighs the box's extra height, and links to the sphere as the most efficient shape.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains that shape decides capacity and quotes the main numbers, but the reasoning about cross-sections is incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: States that the drum holds more without evidence, or suggests that equal surface area means equal volume.

value.criterion: Handling composite solids and real-life application
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Leaves out hidden joined faces in surface area, adds the volumes of the parts, and describes a realistic Kenyan design, explaining which calculation gives sheet and which gives capacity, plus a relevant career.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Handles composite solids mostly correctly and gives a reasonable Kenyan application with some detail missing.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Counts hidden faces or gives no clear real-life application.

records.value: (About 14 minutes.) In groups of 4, learners use a pre-drawn net (or draw their own on manila paper or old cartons) to build one model: a square-based pyramid with a 6 cm square base and four triangular faces (scale model of the 6 m roof, 1 cm = 1 m, vertical height 4 cm). They cut, fold and tape the net, then measure the vertical height (from the apex straight down to the centre of the base) with a ruler and a straight stick, and the slant height (from the apex down the middle of a triangular face to the midpoint of a base edge). They record h = 4 and l = 5 (scale units) and check that 3² + 4² = 5² (the right-angled triangle formed by the vertical height, half the base side and the slant height). They then calculate the area of one triangular face (1/2 x 6 x 5 = 15) and of four faces (60) in a short table with columns: solid, base, h, l, area of one face, number of faces, total.

Learners cut, fold and tape the nets. For model A, they first draw the net, measure a triangular face, and then measure the vertical height (from the apex straight down to the centre of the base) with a ruler and a straight stick, and the slant height (from the apex down the middle of a triangular face to the midpoint of a base edge). They record h = 4 and l = 5 (scale units) and check that 3² + 4² = 5² (the right-angled triangle formed by the vertical height, half the base side, and the slant height). They then calculate the area of one triangular face (1/2 x 6 x 5 = 15), then four faces (60). For model B, they measure the base side (6 cm) and the height of one face (about 5.2 cm), and compute each face as 9√3 ≈ 15.59 cm2. Groups record their measurements in a table with columns: solid, base, h, l, area of one face, number of faces, total.

records.value: (About 12 minutes.) Using their measurements, learners explain to their group and then to the class: (1) why the height of each triangular face is the slant height l and not the vertical height h; (2) how to find l from h and the base side using Pythagoras: l² = h² + (half the base)² = 4² + 3² = 25, so l = 5 m; (3) the rule, using the sentence frame 'Pyramid TSA = base area + the sum of the areas of the triangular faces.' For the roof, the base (the floor of the store) is not covered with iron sheet, so roof area = 4 x 1/2 x 6 x 5 = 60 m2, while a closed pyramid would be 36 + 60 = 96 m2. The teacher supplies the regular triangular pyramid (tetrahedron, all edges 6 cm): each face is 9√3 ≈ 15.59 cm2, so TSA = 4 x 15.59 ≈ 62.35 cm2. In pairs, learners then solve one new problem: a pyramid-shaped roof for a school hall in Kajiado with an 8 m x 8 m base and a vertical height of 3 m (l = 5 m, roof area = 4 x 1/2 x 8 x 5 = 80 m2), and correct their earlier prediction in one sentence, saying what 60 m2 tells us (the material needed) and what it does not (the space inside).

Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 2 learners and push for evidence: 'What did you measure that shows this?' Draw the right-angled triangle (h = 4, half-base = 3, l = 5) on the board and have learners label it. Say: 'Slant height is never called height. We write l for slant and h for vertical.' Introduce the rule only after learners propose it in their own words. Work the 60 m2 example on the board with learners calling out each step and show the tetrahedron result, then have pairs solve the 8 m x 8 m, h = 3 m school hall roof and cold-call 2 pairs for l, a face area and the total. Return to the Predict phase: 'What was the error in the 48 m2 prediction?' Ask: 'If this roof and a box had equal surface area, would they hold the same amount?' to prepare for later volume lessons, without teaching volume now. Note the unit conventions: area in m2, never m or m3.

records.value: (15 min) Groups of 4 work as two pairs at two stations and swap after 7 minutes. Station A (sphere): the football has r = 10.5 cm (the circumference of about 66 cm is given: r = 66 ÷ (2 x 22/7) = 10.5 cm). Learners cover half the ball with strips of paper or masking tape of known width, laid side by side without overlap, peel them off and lay them flat, cut them to fit circles of radius 10.5 cm (area πr² = 346.5 cm2), and count how many circles' worth the half ball used (about 2); doubling gives about 4 for the whole ball. They then compute 4πr² = 4 x 22/7 x 10.5 x 10.5 = 1,386 cm2 and compare with 4 x 346.5 = 1,386 cm2. Station B (composite solid): using a pre-labelled diagram of the Nairobi packaging container (cylinder r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm with a hemisphere on top), learners name the parts (curved cylinder surface, base of the cylinder, hemisphere), mark the circle where the solids meet (r = 7 cm) as 'hidden', and compute: curved cylinder 2πrh = 2 x 22/7 x 7 x 10 = 440 cm2; base πr² = 154 cm2; hemisphere curved 2πr² = 308 cm2.

records.value: (15 min) Groups of 4 split into two pairs with roles (filler, recorder). Pair 1 (prisms): measure the 5 cm x 4 cm x 3 cm rectangular prism model and the triangular prism with 3-4-5 cm right-angled triangle ends and length 10 cm. Record base area and height or length (rectangle 5 x 4 = 20 cm2 base, height 3 cm; triangle 1/2 x 3 x 4 = 6 cm2 base, length 10 cm), then fill each model with dry sand (or water) from a measuring cylinder and record the volume: both hold 60 cm3, so different shapes can have the same volume. Pair 2 (pyramid and prism): take an open pyramid and an open prism with the same square base and the same vertical height, fill the pyramid and pour it into the prism, repeating until the prism is full: 3 pyramid-fuls fill the prism. The pairs then report to each other and complete one shared table of shape, base area, height, base area x height and sand volume (1/3 of that for the pyramid).

records.value: (10 min) Whole class then pairs. Learners use the table to state the rules in their own words: prism volume = base area x height (V = Ah); pyramid volume = 1/3 x base area x height because 3 pyramids fill the prism. Apply: (1) Box from Mzee Kiplagat: base 50 x 50 = 2,500 cm2; height 129 cm; V = 2,500 x 129 = 322,500 cm3 = 322.5 litres (divide by 1,000). (2) Pyramid roof from Lesson 2: base 6 m x 6 m = 36 m2; vertical height 4 m; V = 1/3 x 36 x 4 = 48 m3 = 48,000 litres of air space under the roof, checking that they used the vertical height 4 m and not the slant height 5 m. (3) In one sentence they write the difference: surface area is the material covering the solid (cm2); volume is the space inside it (cm3), so the box's 30,800 cm2 and 322,500 cm3 cannot be compared. Preview: the drum is a cylinder, which is like a prism with a circular base, so V = base area x height should also work; learners write down a prediction for the drum with r = 35 cm and h = 105 cm, but do not calculate it yet because that is Lesson 6.
